column4: The section's dictionary sense for لبد (ل ب د, B003) is one who does not travel or leave; 4:97 challenges people who remain behind by asking whether God's earth was spacious enough for them to migrate. The verse makes staying fixed a question of choice, unlike poverty that restricts movement.

The section's stillness image can describe being unable to move; 4:98 exempts men, women, and children who truly lack means and a way out. It marks the boundary between chosen attachment to the earth and constrained immobility.

The section explains لبد (ل ب د, B001) through felt made as fibers pressed into a layer and also names the person who stays put; 16:80 names wool and animal hair made into furnishings and homes as “سَكَنًا”. The verse supplies the material and dwelling side of that image, though it does not describe the felting process.

The section sets claimed wealth beside the poor person's need and makes giving a route upward; 63:10 urges spending from God's provision before death arrives, when the regretful person wishes for more time to give charity.

The section's man says he spent a mass of wealth, while the needy require compassionate help; 2:262 says spending should not be followed by reminders or injury. In the neighboring charity passage, it distinguishes aid from a self-promoting claim.

The section's ascent depends on turning toward the earthbound poor with mercy; 2:263 says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, defining the manner of aid in the charitable sequence that continues into 2:264.

The section links giving toward the needy with elevation; 2:274 describes spending wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, with reward from God. It continues the same charitable subject as 2:271, adding the steadiness of giving across circumstances.

The section's steep-pass deeds include freeing a neck from bondage; 3:180 says what misers withhold will be put around their necks. It reverses withheld wealth into constriction, opposite the section's act of release.

The section names freeing a captive as part of the passage upward; 24:33 tells owners to help enslaved people seeking emancipation from the property God has given them, making wealth a means of release.

The section treats riches and poverty as a shared earthly condition and makes turning wealth outward a source of ascent; 47:38 says people called to spend who withhold only withhold from themselves, since God is rich and they are needy.

The section contrasts a mass of wealth kept at ground level with the deed that raises a person; 2:261 depicts spending for God as seed bearing seven ears with many grains, turning the spent possession into multiplied yield.

The section opposes piled wealth to giving that carries a person upward; 64:16 urges spending from God's provision and says those protected from their own greed are successful, naming the inward obstacle to releasing wealth.

The section's steep-pass sequence feeds a person in need on a day of hunger; 2:184 makes feeding a poor person an alternative obligation for those who cannot fast, another specific way food reaches the miskīn.
The section makes feeding the needy part of its moral ascent; 5:89 requires feeding ten poor people as one expiation for a broken oath, giving a concrete instance of wealth converted into food.

The section's imagery includes a camel kneeling and feeding the poor; 5:95 includes feeding poor people as an expiation for a hunting violation during pilgrimage, linking a costly animal-related act to provision for those in need.

The section names feeding the hungry and the poor as the steep-pass work; 22:28 tells pilgrims to eat from sacrificial livestock and feed the needy who ask, an earlier formulation in the same sacrificial passage as 22:36.

The section sets amassed wealth beside people in need; 4:8 says that when inheritance is being divided and relatives, orphans, and poor people are present, they should be given something from it, directing property toward those with little.
The section's lexicon says a bird can be لبد (ل ب د, B003), crouched on the ground; 16:79 instead points to birds held in the sky, a specific reversal from the grounded bird to one borne aloft.

The section places a rich man and a poor person on the same earthly plane; 16:71 asks why people given more provision do not share it with those under their authority, presenting unequal provision as a relationship of withheld goods.

The section distinguishes earthly wealth from the ascent made through mercy and help; 43:32 says God apportions provision and raises some people above others in worldly ranks, yet God's mercy is better than what they accumulate.

The section's settled-place and wealth imagery meets people made poor by displacement; 59:8 describes needy emigrants driven from their homes and property who seek God's bounty. It supplies the migrants' own loss that 59:9's generosity answers.
The section's wealthy man boasts of having spent “مَالًا لُّبَدًا”; 18:34 gives the garden owner’s comparison, “أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا”, making wealth a basis for status over another person.

The section places abundant wealth beside the poor person's earth-bound state; 18:35 has the garden owner enter his property convinced it will never perish, exposing the false permanence that the section's grave and soil senses unsettle.

The section's dictionary also gives the reversal “no little or much” for לبد (ل ب د, B007); 18:42 depicts the garden owner's fruit and wealth destroyed, leaving him regretful over what he had spent. The former abundance collapses toward nothing.
